column7: Tarleton should resist approaching AI as primarily a technology initiative. It is an institutional transformation that will require clear leadership, governance, faculty development, appropriate infrastructure, and measurable outcomes. We should establish university-wide expectations for AI competency while allowing disciplines to define what meaningful and responsible AI use looks like in their fields. Our greatest opportunity for differentiation may be in applied AI—particularly agriculture, rural healthcare, small business and entrepreneurship, education, and workforce development. The challenge will be moving beyond isolated pilots and individual enthusiasm toward coordinated, scalable implementation while maintaining appropriate attention to ethics, academic integrity, data security, and the human judgment that should remain at the center of a Tarleton education.

Reposting my response to #5 here because I do think it’s central to a practical vision. 

Equip the faculty and staff. Everything else hinges on sound and effective decision making. There is obviously a fair amount of ai use on campus among employees but some of it is undisciplined and at times counterproductive because the owner let AI lead with the ideas and didn’t fully own the product. We can’t blame AI when the product is sloppy … if we do that, we acknowledge that we’ve relinquished ownership and are replaceable. The ai should assist employees. We have to own the technology, not vice versa. Ai can replace undisciplined users. It can’t replace talented employees disciplined at its use. That notion applies to the future of our students as well. Training and education should be our early priority I’d suggest…. But we do have to support a small segment of users that keep Tarleton State ahead of others in the higher ed marketplace.

column7:
Tarleton State should approach AI as an organizational change initiative, not simply a technology implementation. My research found that faculty are already engaging with AI, but they are doing so amid unclear expectations, uneven access to support, and differing interpretations of responsible use. Faculty concerns are often pedagogical and ethical rather than evidence of resistance to innovation. I recommend establishing institution-wide guardrails for privacy, transparency, academic integrity, accountability, and ethical use while preserving disciplinary flexibility. These expectations should be developed through faculty and staff listening sessions, cross-disciplinary dialogue, and ongoing review rather than through top-down policy alone.

Professional learning should be sustained, peer-led, discipline-sensitive, practice-based, and accessible across campuses and appointment types. A tiered learning model, Faculty AI Fellows program, communities of practice, and centralized resource repository could help build institutional capacity. Major challenges will include inconsistent expectations, initiative fatigue, unequal access to time and resources, concerns about professional identity, data privacy, and the risk of implementing AI tools before establishing clear educational purposes and measures of effectiveness.
